newsitem.title: UK: World refiners comfortable despite drop in margins.
newsitem.headline: World refiners comfortable despite drop in margins.

text.p: World refinery operators enjoyed comfortable margins last week despite a continuing fall in profit levels from early April highs.
"Nobody is worried yet," said one European refiner. "Margins were exceptional and they've now come back to something I would consider as more normal."
Complex refineries in Asia, still the world's most lucrative, last week made less than $5 a barrel of profit from processing Dubai crude for the first time since February.
However last week's average return of $4.95, according to Reuters calculations using standard product yields, still added almost 30 percent to the value of the processed crude.

An Asian hydroskimming plant averaged a return of $2.25 a barrel last week partly because the price of gas oil has come off its peak, with traders worried that the dominant buyer's spending spree may have come to an end.
With product prices in the Mediterranean on a slide, margins for less sophisticated local plant running Ural crude fell to 69 cents a barrel on Friday and an average of $1.10 for the week.

In the highly competitive north European market a less sophisticated hydroskimming refinery running more expensive Brent made just 53 cents a barrel on Friday, down from a high of $1.38 in early April but well above February lows.
"It's nothing more significant than a narrowing differential between crude and products," said the European refiner.
The price of benchmark north sea dated Brent pegged up 30 cents last week, on the back of buying by refiners eager to run at full capacity while margins stay healthy.
"There has been a good pull of gas oil to the East which has helped keep north-west Europe up, despite the over-capacity here," said one oil products trader.

He anticipated margins staying rosy for at least another month, even if the boisterous Asian gas oil market becomes subdued. By end-May summer gasoline demand from the U.S. would be lending support, he suggested.
For Europe, the biggest worry was the continuing fall in demand for fuel oil, particularly the one percent sulphur grade, which has hit margins hard all year.
He predicted returns on fuel oil destruction and upgrading plant would continue to grow.

The sharp fall in margin numbers through last week in Asia, the Mediterrranean and Europe was mirrored in the United States, where plants running key domestic grade West Texas Intermediate made 72 cents profit a barrel on Friday.
The week's average for processing WTI was 93 cents. U.S. plants running North Sea crudes made $1.68 a barrel on Friday. -- Sean Maguire, London newsroom +44 171 542 8060
